description: We are a team of three Engineering students passionate about data analytics, problem-solving, and innovation. Our skills include data analysis, statistical methods, multi-criteria decision-making, optimization, and process improvement. We are interested in using NASA Earth observation data to develop practical, data-driven solutions to real-world challenges. We value teamwork, creativity, and an analytical approach.

details:
Burning Activity Calendar

Project Overview

Burning Activity Calendar is an interactive web application supported by a data harmonization workflow designed to make satellite-detected fire activity more comparable across different sensors and over time.

Long-term fire analysis faces a major challenge: satellite instruments do not detect hotspots in exactly the same way. NASA's MODIS instrument observes active fires at approximately 1 km resolution, while VIIRS provides observations at 375 m resolution. VIIRS can detect smaller and less intense thermal anomalies that MODIS may miss. Consequently, combining their raw hotspot counts can create artificial discontinuities in historical records.

Our project addresses this issue by developing a monthly harmonization method that converts historical MODIS observations to a VIIRS-equivalent scale. We transformed this method into an interactive calendar that allows users to explore fire activity over time, examine regional patterns, and understand the uncertainty associated with historical estimates.

How Does It Work?

1. Data Collection and Preparation

We collected approximately 1.26 million active fire detections from NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) for our Türkiye pilot. The dataset combines MODIS observations from Terra and Aqua, VIIRS observations from Suomi-NPP, and VIIRS observations from NOAA-20. The resulting time series covers November 2000 to November 2026, comprising 313 months.

We processed the observations, checked for duplicate detections, and addressed persistent non-fire heat sources such as industrial facilities and gas flares. We also evaluated our static-source filtering approach against 2025 observations to understand how effectively it identifies persistent heat sources and how often it may remove genuine fire detections.

2. Sensor Harmonization

We used the overlapping observation period between MODIS and VIIRS, from February 2012 to December 2025, to measure differences in their detection counts.

The overall VIIRS-to-MODIS hotspot ratio was approximately 3.38. However, this relationship varied substantially by calendar month, ranging from 1.82 in May to 4.77 in September.

Instead of applying one fixed correction factor, we calculated a separate factor for each calendar month using aggregated observations across the overlap period. We then applied these factors to historical MODIS counts to estimate their VIIRS-equivalent values.

The earliest part of the record required additional treatment. From November 2000 to June 2002, only the Terra satellite was available. We therefore derived separate Terra-only factors and assigned these months a low-confidence label.

3. Model Validation and Uncertainty

We compared three harmonization approaches: a single factor for all months, a log-log model, and separate factors for each calendar month.

To evaluate their performance, we used leave-one-year-out cross-validation. We repeatedly excluded one overlap year, recalculated the factors using the remaining years, and compared the predicted counts with the actual VIIRS observations for the excluded year.

The monthly-factor approach performed best, achieving 13% pooled monthly Weighted Absolute Percentage Error (WAPE) and 4% annual Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE). During the main fire season, from June to October, monthly WAPE was 11%.

We also developed empirical uncertainty ranges based on validation errors. Since prediction errors behaved differently during and outside the fire season, we calculated separate ranges for these periods. Each historical estimate is accompanied by an uncertainty range and a confidence label, helping users distinguish direct satellite observations from converted historical estimates.

What Does the Web Application Offer?

The web application makes the harmonized dataset accessible through an interactive interface.

Users can:

  • Explore the Türkiye pilot at national level, select one of seven geographic regions, or define a custom area using latitude and longitude coordinates.
  • View monthly hotspot distributions on a 0.1-degree spatial grid.
  • Explore a year-by-month calendar covering the full 26-year record.
  • Select a month and compare its activity with the historical median for the same calendar month.
  • Review confidence labels and uncertainty ranges for historical estimates.
  • Compare long-term activity between selected periods.
  • Examine seasonal patterns and download the displayed data as a CSV file.

We deliberately chose the historical median rather than the mean for monthly comparisons because exceptionally active fire periods can distort average values. We also selected a square-root colour scale after testing linear and logarithmic alternatives. This provides a balance between displaying extreme fire activity and keeping less active months visible.

Results and Transferability

The harmonized series removes the artificial increase observed around 2012 in the raw hotspot record. It also preserves important historical activity that would be lost if analysis started only with VIIRS observations.

Our analysis identifies 2009 as the most active year in the Türkiye pilot. September 2011 is the most active month, with an estimated 27,261 hotspots and an uncertainty range of 23,161 to 35,107.

The results also reveal substantial regional differences. For example, during July 2021, the month of the Manavgat fire, the Mediterranean region recorded approximately eleven times its usual July median. This demonstrates why regional exploration is important alongside national statistics.

To examine whether the workflow could be applied beyond the pilot, we ran the same code on approximately 3.6 million detections from Argentina for 2012–2025. The monthly-factor approach achieved 9% monthly validation error in Argentina, compared with 13% pooled monthly WAPE in the Türkiye pilot. The monthly conversion patterns differed between the two countries, indicating that the workflow can be transferred, but calibration factors should be calculated separately for each location.

Tools and Technologies

We developed the data-processing workflow in Python using Google Colab. The main libraries included pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, Plotly, GeoPandas, Shapely, and Requests. Microsoft Excel was used for an independent manual check of selected conversion factors.

The interactive application was developed with Streamlit and deployed through Streamlit Community Cloud. GitHub hosts the project's code and supporting files.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Burning Activity Calendar provides a more consistent basis for examining long-term satellite-detected fire activity. By addressing sensor-related discontinuities, retaining earlier observations, and communicating uncertainty, it helps users avoid interpreting changes in detection technology as changes in fire activity.

The application is intended to support researchers, analysts, environmental organizations, and people interested in understanding historical fire patterns. Its interactive regional exploration can help identify unusual periods and spatial differences that may be hidden in national totals.

Our approach is designed to be adaptable to additional countries and future satellite observations. Further work could include comparison with official fire statistics, integration of NOAA-21 observations, and analysis using Fire Radiative Power (FRP).

Our goal is not simply to count hotspots, but to make long-term satellite fire observations more comparable, transparent, and useful for understanding changes across time and space.

Project Showcase

1. Interactive Fire Activity Map and 26-Year Calendar

The main application interface brings together a spatial hotspot map and a 26-year monthly activity calendar. Users can explore harmonized fire activity across Türkiye, select different regions and time periods, and identify spatial and seasonal patterns.

2. Historical Comparison and Seasonal Analysis

The analysis dashboard provides historical context for each selected month. It compares current activity with historical medians, displays confidence levels, and visualizes seasonal patterns alongside empirical uncertainty ranges. This helps users distinguish unusually active periods from typical variation.
